screens.title: Design by Contract (DbC)
screens.narratorSegment: Design by Contract turns programs into a network of promises. Each routine gets a short written agreement: the caller promises certain conditions before calling, the routine guarantees outcomes after it runs, and the object promises certain invariants always hold. This chapter uses the vending machine and a small Wallet example to make these ideas concrete. You will learn how preconditions protect implementers from invalid callers, how postconditions document the routine's guarantees, and how invariants keep an object's state coherent across operations. We'll also show practical implementation with assertions and type hints, explain when to use defensive checks at system boundaries, and highlight the common traps such as relying on assertions for user-facing validation or assuming assertions always run in production. By the end of this lesson you should be able to state clear contracts for simple classes, use assertions to detect programming errors during development, and design unit tests that validate contract behavior. As you watch the code walkthrough, notice how small assertions reduce debugging time and clarify intent — what contract would you write for a method you use every day?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: DbC makes software behavior explicit: preconditions, postconditions, and invariants are small, testable promises that improve correctness, debugging, and documentation.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Design by Contract
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Design by Contract

Define clear obligations for callers, guarantees for routines, and invariants that keep state consistent. This improves debugging and makes code intent explicit.

Why this matters

When contracts are explicit, failures point to a broken promise instead of an obscure bug. Tests map naturally to contracts, and reviewers can read expectations directly in code.

  • Catch programming errors close to the source.
  • Clarify responsibilities between caller and routine.
  • Improve tests by turning contracts into test cases.
Analogy: A vending machine contract
Outcome: Guarantees you get the snack or a clear error
Warning: Contracts are not user input validation
In this lesson
Core elements
Preconditions, postconditions, invariants — the heart of DbC.
Implementation
Use assertions and type hints to document and check contracts.
Pitfalls & testing
Don't use asserts for expected user errors; prefer exceptions at boundaries.
Explore Key Topics
Preconditions
Caller promises required inputs. If violated, the caller is at fault.
Invariants
State rules that must hold outside method execution windows.
Assertions
Development-time checks that fail fast on broken contracts.

screens.title: What is Design by Contract?
screens.narratorSegment: Design by Contract frames each software routine as a brief agreement between the caller and the implementation. The caller agrees to meet preconditions before invoking a routine, and the routine agrees to satisfy postconditions when it returns. Invariants are promises the object keeps continuously, except while a method runs. Think of a vending machine: you insert coins and select an item — your precondition is the correct amount and selection, the machine's postcondition is that you receive the item or clear feedback, and its invariant is that it never dispenses more products than it contains. DbC helps developers by replacing implicit assumptions with explicit, small checks. These checks document intent and make debugging faster because a failing assertion points directly to the broken promise. A common misconception is that DbC removes all validation; it does not. DbC clarifies where validation belongs: user input needs boundary checks, while internal routines rely on their callers to satisfy preconditions. In practice, DbC encourages a collaborative mindset between components where responsibilities are declared and checked, and that clarity is what makes systems more robust and easier to reason about. What promise would you write for the method you most often call?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: DbC is a programming approach that treats routines as contracts: preconditions, postconditions, and invariants define obligations and guarantees.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › What is DbC?
Definition

Contract elements

  • Preconditions: obligations the caller must meet before calling.
  • Postconditions: guarantees the routine must provide on success.
  • Invariants: facts that remain true about an object across operations.
Metaphor
A vending machine contract: insert correct coins and select a valid slot; the machine dispenses the product and updates stock; stock never becomes negative.
Why it helps

Making assumptions explicit reduces debugging time because failed assertions explain which promise was broken. Contracts double as documentation and test specifications.

Concrete example
A deposit method can assert amount > 0 as a precondition, and that balance increased by amount as a postcondition.
Key takeaway
Contracts are short, testable promises — not a replacement for input sanitation at system boundaries.

screens.title: Preconditions: the caller's promises
screens.narratorSegment: Preconditions describe what the caller must guarantee before invoking a routine. They protect implementations from checking every input and let callers know their responsibilities. For example, a divide function might have a precondition that the denominator is not zero. In a Wallet example, deposit(amount) should require amount > 0; withdraw(amount) should require both amount > 0 and sufficient balance. Preconditions are especially valuable when many callers exist: a single assertion centralizes the requirement instead of duplicating checks everywhere. In practice, preconditions are best enforced with assertions during development so violations indicate programming errors, not user mistakes. However, when inputs come from untrusted sources — a web form or external A P I — preconditions should be guarded by boundary validation and converted into safe errors before entering the trusted core. A common misconception is to use assertions for expected runtime errors; instead, use exceptions or validation routines for user-facing input. When you write a precondition, think about who can fix the violation: if the caller can, it belongs as a precondition; if the runtime must handle unpredictable external input, handle it before the contract. Can you name a method you call that should assert non-empty strings as a precondition?

keyIdea.title: Preconditions
keyIdea.text: Preconditions state what callers must do before invoking a routine; use assertions during development and boundary checks for untrusted input.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Preconditions
Core claim

Caller obligations

Preconditions document expectations about parameters and state before execution. A failed precondition points to caller error.

Example
withdraw(amount) requires amount > 0 and balance >= amount. Assert these at the start of the method during development.
Misconception
Don't use assertions to handle predictable user input; use validation and user-friendly errors at boundaries.
Checklist for preconditions
  • Is the caller responsible for fixing the violation?
  • Can you detect the violation cheaply at method entry?
  • Would an assertion help developers diagnose a bug quickly?
Key Takeaway

Write preconditions for developer-correctable issues and validate untrusted inputs at system boundaries.

screens.title: Postconditions: what the routine guarantees
screens.narratorSegment: Postconditions are promises the routine itself makes after completing successfully. They state the expected result and any state modifications. For example, after deposit(amount) the postcondition is that balance increased by amount; after withdraw(amount) the postcondition is that balance decreased by amount. Implement postconditions as assertions after the operation to ensure logic produced the expected change. They are particularly helpful when operations are complex or when side effects must be precise, because a failing postcondition tells you the implementation did not fulfill its promise. One subtle point is to use postconditions only for successful completion — if a method returns an error or raises an exception, postconditions need not hold. Another misconception is to duplicate checks that belong to postconditions as defensive pre-checks; instead, separate responsibilities: preconditions validate input and environment, while postconditions validate the routine's result. When writing postconditions, store any necessary original state and assert the relationship explicitly. A short learning task is to write a postcondition for a transfer method that ensures two account balances update correctly and the total remains constant. Postconditions: what the routine guarantees means postconditions confirm a routine's result and side effects after successful execution; assert them to verify implementation correctness.. In practical terms, check outcomes and state changes after successful execution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Postconditions confirm a routine's result and side effects after successful execution; assert them to verify implementation correctness.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Postconditions
Guarantees

What must be true on success

Postconditions state the expected result and how the state should have changed. They help detect implementation bugs where intended effects are not realized.

Example
For deposit: record original_balance, perform addition, then assert balance == original_balance + amount.
When to assert postconditions
  • After modifications complete and before returning.
  • Only for successful paths; errors or exceptions can bypass them.
  • Use them to document behavior and to make unit tests precise.
Key Takeaway

Postconditions verify that the routine delivered its promised result; use them to catch logic errors quickly.

screens.title: Invariants: preserving object integrity
screens.narratorSegment: Invariants are properties that remain true for an object's lifetime, except possibly during the internal execution of a method. They capture class-level integrity rules such as 'balance never negative' or 'account number is a 10-digit string'. Invariants must be checked at consistent points, for example at the end of constructors and the end of public methods, to ensure the object remains valid. When using assertions for invariants during development, place checks at method entry and exit so temporary internal violations are allowed while a routine runs, but the external contract still holds. Invariants are particularly useful for catching subtle bugs that arise from multiple operations combined. A common mistake is to assume an invariant without enforcing it after complex updates; a single assertion after a series of updates will reveal whether the object's internal logic preserved its integrity. Also remember that invariants can inform A P I design: if an object promises a never-negative balance, callers can make stronger assumptions and simplify their logic. Think about invariants for structures you use daily — what core guarantees would make their use safer and easier to test?

keyIdea.title: Invariants
keyIdea.text: Invariants are class-wide rules that should hold outside of method execution windows and protect object integrity across operations.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Invariants
Object integrity

What invariants do

They keep the object's internal model consistent across operations, enabling safer assumptions by callers and clearer tests for implementers.

Example
For Wallet, invariant: balance >= 0. Check after constructor and after public methods that might change balance.
Best practices
  • Assert invariants at object creation and at the end of public methods.
  • Allow temporary internal invariant violations but re-establish them before returning.
  • Document invariants so tests can assert them explicitly.
Key Takeaway

Invariants reduce error surface by keeping an object's essential properties consistent across operations.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Implementing DbC
Code walkthrough
# wallet.py - Refactored Code with DbC
class Wallet:
  def __init__(self, initial_balance: float):
    # Invariant: balance must be non-negative
    assert initial_balance >= 0, "Initial balance cannot be negative."
    self.balance: float = initial_balance
    assert self.balance >= 0, "Invariant violated after __init__: balance is negative."

  def deposit(self, amount: float) -> None:
    # Precondition
    assert amount > 0, "Deposit amount must be positive."
    # Invariant before
    assert self.balance >= 0, "Invariant violated before deposit: balance negative."

    original_balance = self.balance
    self.balance += amount

    # Postcondition
    assert self.balance == original_balance + amount, "Postcondition violated: balance mismatch."
    # Invariant after
    assert self.balance >= 0, "Invariant violated after deposit: balance negative."

  def withdraw(self, amount: float) -> None:
    # Preconditions
    assert amount > 0, "Withdrawal amount must be positive."
    assert self.balance >= amount, "Precondition violated: Insufficient funds."
    assert self.balance >= 0, "Invariant violated before withdraw: balance negative."

    original_balance = self.balance
    self.balance -= amount

    # Postcondition
    assert self.balance == original_balance - amount, "Postcondition violated: balance mismatch."
    assert self.balance >= 0, "Invariant violated after withdraw: balance negative."
Explanation bullets
  • Type hints make intended types explicit and aid tooling.
  • Preconditions are asserted before changes.
  • Postconditions are asserted after to confirm effects.
  • Invariants checked consistently to maintain integrity.
Concrete test idea
Write a test that calls withdraw with amount greater than balance and assert that an assertion triggers during development.
Key Takeaway

Assertions plus type hints form a concise and testable contract during development; critical runtime checks still require explicit error handling.

screens.title: DbC vs Defensive Programming
screens.narratorSegment: DbC and defensive programming share the goal of reliable software but differ in responsibility and placement of checks. Defensive programming validates inputs everywhere, making each routine robust against any caller. DbC, by contrast, separates duties: callers must satisfy preconditions and the routine can assume them in the trusted core. Use defensive checks at system boundaries such as HTTP handlers, message consumers, or CLI parsers — these handle untrusted input. Use DbC within the internal code base where callers are known and tests can exercise contract violations. The practical result: DbC reduces duplicated checks inside trusted code paths and clarifies APIs, while defensive checks protect against malicious or malformed inputs at entry points. A common pitfall is to flip expectations: using assertions for user-facing validation will produce poor user experience and brittle production behavior when assertions are disabled. Conversely, over-defensive internal code duplicates logic and obscures intent. The balance is to sanitize at the boundary, then use contracts inside to make behavior explicit and tests precise. Ask yourself: which layer handles the first validation for requests in your current project? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › DbC vs Defensive
Defensive Programming

Every routine validates inputs

Pros: safer against all callers. Cons: duplicated checks and blurred responsibilities.

When to use
At external boundaries and when inputs are untrusted or ambiguous.
Design by Contract

Clear caller vs callee responsibilities

Pros: fewer duplicated checks, clearer APIs, faster debugging. Cons: requires discipline and clear boundary validation.

When to use
Inside trusted modules where callers are expected to follow documented contracts.
Concrete hybrid approach
  • Validate and sanitize at system edges (parse, reject, or coerce user input).
  • Convert sanitized input into domain objects and enter the trusted core.
  • Inside core modules, rely on DbC: assert preconditions and invariants and test contract violations.
Key Takeaway

Use boundary validation for untrusted input and DbC internally to keep code concise and testable.

screens.title: Where to place checks in a system
screens.narratorSegment: A practical pattern is: sanitize at the boundary, convert to domain types, then enforce contracts within the core. First, parse and validate raw external input using explicit checks and user-friendly errors. Next, convert validated input to domain objects using constructors or factory functions — this is where you coerce types and make invariants explicit. Finally, within your application's core, rely on preconditions, postconditions, and invariants expressed with assertions and type hints. This flow minimizes duplicated checks and keeps user-facing code resilient. If an assertion fails inside the core during testing, it signals a programming error or a missed boundary check. →

screens.title: Pitfalls: assertions, production, and over-asserting
screens.narratorSegment: DbC is powerful but can be misapplied. First, don't use assertions for expected user errors. Assertions are for programming errors — situations your code never expects in normal operation. When user input is wrong, return a clear error or raise a proper exception; that preserves user experience. Second, be aware that assertions may be disabled in production builds, so any critical runtime checks must be implemented with always-on logic, for example raising exceptions after explicit if checks. Third, avoid over-asserting trivial conditions that add noise and reduce signal. Adding assertions for every tiny intermediate property can obscure the meaningful contract checks. Instead, assert the critical preconditions, postconditions, and invariants that materially affect correctness. Finally, do not conflate defensive checks and contracts: use defensive validation at boundaries and DbC in the core. A useful test strategy is to include negative tests that intentionally violate preconditions — these tests verify that contracts detect programmer mistakes and remain informative. Think about one assertion in your code that could be converted into a clearer contract and one that should be handled by user-facing validation instead.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Pitfalls

Common mistakes

  • Assertions for user errors: leads to poor UX and brittle production if assertions are disabled.
  • Disabled assertions: don't rely on assert for checks that must run in production.
  • Over-asserting: too many trivial assertions hide the important ones and reduce signal.
Example mistake
Using assert to validate a web form email will crash the server for normal user mistakes instead of returning friendly errors.
Mitigation
Reserve assertions for developer-detectable contract violations; use exceptions or validation libraries at boundaries; document and test contracts thoroughly.
Key Takeaway

Treat assertions as a developer tool and ensure critical checks are always executed in production via explicit error handling.

screens.title: Testing contracts: map contracts to unit tests
screens.narratorSegment: Contracts are a natural source for unit tests. For preconditions, write negative tests that intentionally violate the contract and expect a failure — for example, calling withdraw with an amount greater than balance should trigger a contract violation during development. For postconditions, write positive tests that observe the expected result, such as verifying the balance increased by the deposit amount. For invariants, assert them after sequences of operations to ensure complex interactions keep the object consistent. Tests derived from contracts serve three purposes: they verify the implementation, they document intended behavior for reviewers, and they alert you when refactors break promises. When assertions are used to enforce contracts, unit tests should run in an environment where assertions are enabled so they can catch violations. For production-grade tests, also include tests that simulate boundary validation and expected error handling for user input. One recommended pattern is to keep contract tests focused on developer-facing guarantees and separate boundary tests that cover user-facing validation paths. Which contract-derived test would you add first for your own project? screens.title: Live coding: refactor the Wallet
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a live refactor of the starter Wallet. Begin by annotating initial_balance, amount parameters, and method return types. Add an invariant assertion in the constructor to prevent negative initial balances. For deposit, assert amount > 0, check the invariant before modifying state, record the original balance, update balance, then assert the postcondition that the balance equals original plus amount and that invariant still holds. For withdraw, assert amount > 0 and that balance is sufficient before changing state. After the change, assert the expected decreased balance and the invariant. Run the script with valid calls to observe normal behavior. Then intentionally trigger violations: try deposit(-20) to see the deposit precondition fail and withdraw(150) when balance is lower to see the insufficient funds precondition fail. These failures point exactly to the broken contract during development. Be mindful that in production you may convert some assertions into exceptions so checks cannot be disabled. For your practice, refactor the starter code, run the script, and then write two unit tests: one that succeeds and one that triggers a precondition violation. Which failing test gave you the clearest message?

Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Refactor: Wallet
Starter to refactored
# Starter snippet
class Wallet:
  def __init__(self, initial_balance):
    self.balance = initial_balance

  def deposit(self, amount):
    self.balance += amount

  def withdraw(self, amount):
    if self.balance >= amount:
      self.balance -= amount

# After refactor: add type hints and assertions (see previous code walkthrough)
Activity steps
  1. Add type hints to all methods and attributes.
  2. Add invariant check in constructor: initial_balance >= 0.
  3. Assert preconditions in deposit and withdraw.
  4. Assert postconditions for balance changes.
  5. Run valid and invalid cases and write two unit tests.
Pro tip

When a test fails, the assertion message should make clear which contract failed and why — include a short explanatory string in assert statements.

screens.title: API design and documenting contracts
screens.narratorSegment: Contracts belong in your A P I documentation and in code. When designing methods, state preconditions and postconditions in docstrings and in code via type hints and assertions so both humans and tools can consume the contract. For public APIs, prefer explicit validation at the boundary with clear error types and messages. For internal APIs, include concise assert statements and short docstrings that describe the contract in one or two sentences. This makes code reviews faster because reviewers see required caller behavior and can judge whether callers satisfy it. Document invariants in class-level docstrings and enforce them with tests. Also consider compatibility: when evolving an A P I, think about whether changing a contract breaks existing callers — if so, bump a major version or provide a migration path. Use contract-based tests to detect incompatible changes automatically. Finally, keep assertion messages actionable: a message like "Precondition violated: amount must be positive" points exactly to the fix. Good contract documentation reduces cross-team misunderstandings and accelerates safe refactoring. screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: Remember three central ideas: First, Design by Contract makes expectations explicit with preconditions, postconditions, and invariants. Third, contracts and defensive checks are complementary: validate untrusted input at system boundaries, then rely on contracts inside your trusted core. fullNarratorScript:
Design by Contract turns programs into a network of promises. Each routine gets a short written agreement: the caller promises certain conditions before calling, the routine guarantees outcomes after it runs, and the object promises certain invariants always hold. This chapter uses the vending machine and a small Wallet example to make these ideas concrete. You will learn how preconditions protect implementers from invalid callers, how postconditions document the routine's guarantees, and how invariants keep an object's state coherent across operations. We'll also show practical implementation with assertions and type hints, explain when to use defensive checks at system boundaries, and highlight the common traps such as relying on assertions for user-facing validation or assuming assertions always run in production. By the end of this lesson you should be able to state clear contracts for simple classes, use assertions to detect programming errors during development, and design unit tests that validate contract behavior. As you watch the code walkthrough, notice how small assertions reduce debugging time and clarify intent — what contract would you write for a method you use every day?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to name and apply the three contract elements: precondition, postcondition, and invariant. You will practice expressing these contracts for small classes and functions, turning them into assertions and type hints that make assumptions explicit. You'll also learn when to check input defensively at system boundaries and when the contract-based approach is a clearer option in the trusted core. A key objective is to use contracts as specifications for unit tests, making tests more precise and meaningful. Lastly, you will identify common errors such as using assertions for expected user input and over-asserting trivial conditions, and learn safer alternatives like raising exceptions for runtime user errors. These skills improve debugging speed and make APIs easier to document and review. Picture yourself writing a deposit method: you will state the precondition, code the postcondition check, and assert the invariant — then write tests that confirm each promise. That hands-on experience is the bridge from understanding to reliable practice.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice: you'll add type hints across methods to clarify expected types, write assertions for preconditions and invariants, and convert contracts into unit test cases that assert precondition violations and postcondition results. You will also practice refactoring a simple Wallet class to include initial invariants and method-level assertions. In that exercise, you'll see how an assertion pinpointing a negative initial balance immediately surfaces a bug that would otherwise spread through the system. We will contrast assertions with explicit exception-based checks used at boundaries like web A P I handlers, and you'll learn how to document contracts so reviewers and consumers understand responsibilities. Finally, you will get a short assessment that asks you to propose preconditions and postconditions for a ShoppingCart method and to explain how to enforce a User email invariant safely. These objectives map directly to common developer workflows: code, review, test, and deploy with fewer surprises. Imagine writing tests that intentionally violate preconditions to confirm your system fails fast and clearly.

Design by Contract frames each software routine as a brief agreement between the caller and the implementation. The caller agrees to meet preconditions before invoking a routine, and the routine agrees to satisfy postconditions when it returns. Invariants are promises the object keeps continuously, except while a method runs. Think of a vending machine: you insert coins and select an item — your precondition is the correct amount and selection, the machine's postcondition is that you receive the item or clear feedback, and its invariant is that it never dispenses more products than it contains. DbC helps developers by replacing implicit assumptions with explicit, small checks. These checks document intent and make debugging faster because a failing assertion points directly to the broken promise. A common misconception is that DbC removes all validation; it does not. DbC clarifies where validation belongs: user input needs boundary checks, while internal routines rely on their callers to satisfy preconditions. In practice, DbC encourages a collaborative mindset between components where responsibilities are declared and checked, and that clarity is what makes systems more robust and easier to reason about. What promise would you write for the method you most often call?

Preconditions describe what the caller must guarantee before invoking a routine. They protect implementations from checking every input and let callers know their responsibilities. For example, a divide function might have a precondition that the denominator is not zero. In a Wallet example, deposit(amount) should require amount > 0; withdraw(amount) should require both amount > 0 and sufficient balance. Preconditions are especially valuable when many callers exist: a single assertion centralizes the requirement instead of duplicating checks everywhere. In practice, preconditions are best enforced with assertions during development so violations indicate programming errors, not user mistakes. However, when inputs come from untrusted sources — a web form or external A P I — preconditions should be guarded by boundary validation and converted into safe errors before entering the trusted core. A common misconception is to use assertions for expected runtime errors; instead, use exceptions or validation routines for user-facing input. When you write a precondition, think about who can fix the violation: if the caller can, it belongs as a precondition; if the runtime must handle unpredictable external input, handle it before the contract. Can you name a method you call that should assert non-empty strings as a precondition?

Postconditions are promises the routine itself makes after completing successfully. They state the expected result and any state modifications. For example, after deposit(amount) the postcondition is that balance increased by amount; after withdraw(amount) the postcondition is that balance decreased by amount. Implement postconditions as assertions after the operation to ensure logic produced the expected change. They are particularly helpful when operations are complex or when side effects must be precise, because a failing postcondition tells you the implementation did not fulfill its promise. One subtle point is to use postconditions only for successful completion — if a method returns an error or raises an exception, postconditions need not hold. Another misconception is to duplicate checks that belong to postconditions as defensive pre-checks; instead, separate responsibilities: preconditions validate input and environment, while postconditions validate the routine's result. When writing postconditions, store any necessary original state and assert the relationship explicitly. A short learning task is to write a postcondition for a transfer method that ensures two account balances update correctly and the total remains constant. Postconditions: what the routine guarantees means postconditions confirm a routine's result and side effects after successful execution; assert them to verify implementation correctness.. In practical terms, check outcomes and state changes after successful execution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Invariants are properties that remain true for an object's lifetime, except possibly during the internal execution of a method. They capture class-level integrity rules such as 'balance never negative' or 'account number is a 10-digit string'. Invariants must be checked at consistent points, for example at the end of constructors and the end of public methods, to ensure the object remains valid. When using assertions for invariants during development, place checks at method entry and exit so temporary internal violations are allowed while a routine runs, but the external contract still holds. Invariants are particularly useful for catching subtle bugs that arise from multiple operations combined. A common mistake is to assume an invariant without enforcing it after complex updates; a single assertion after a series of updates will reveal whether the object's internal logic preserved its integrity. Also remember that invariants can inform A P I design: if an object promises a never-negative balance, callers can make stronger assumptions and simplify their logic. Think about invariants for structures you use daily — what core guarantees would make their use safer and easier to test?

Now we'll implement contracts in code using a Wallet example. Start by adding type hints to clarify parameter and return types. Then add assertions for invariants in the constructor, preconditions at method entry, and postconditions after updates. Use an assertion before and after a method to check the invariant holds across the call. For deposit, assert amount > 0, record original_balance, add amount, then assert balance increased by amount and invariant preserved. For withdraw, assert amount > 0 and balance >= amount as preconditions, perform the subtraction, and assert the postcondition. During development, these assertions fail fast and point to either caller mistakes or implementation bugs. Keep in mind that assertions can be disabled in production, so critical runtime checks should use explicit exceptions when needed. After you read it, run the starter script to observe assertion errors when contract violations are triggered. Remember: assertions are for programming errors; boundary validation should be handled where the input enters your system. Implementing DbC: assertions and type hints means use type hints for clarity, assert preconditions at entry, assert postconditions after state changes, and check invariants at entry and exit.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

DbC and defensive programming share the goal of reliable software but differ in responsibility and placement of checks. Defensive programming validates inputs everywhere, making each routine robust against any caller. DbC, by contrast, separates duties: callers must satisfy preconditions and the routine can assume them in the trusted core. Use defensive checks at system boundaries such as HTTP handlers, message consumers, or CLI parsers — these handle untrusted input. Use DbC within the internal code base where callers are known and tests can exercise contract violations. The practical result: DbC reduces duplicated checks inside trusted code paths and clarifies APIs, while defensive checks protect against malicious or malformed inputs at entry points. A common pitfall is to flip expectations: using assertions for user-facing validation will produce poor user experience and brittle production behavior when assertions are disabled. Conversely, over-defensive internal code duplicates logic and obscures intent. The balance is to sanitize at the boundary, then use contracts inside to make behavior explicit and tests precise. Ask yourself: which layer handles the first validation for requests in your current project? The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

DbC is powerful but can be misapplied. First, don't use assertions for expected user errors. Assertions are for programming errors — situations your code never expects in normal operation. When user input is wrong, return a clear error or raise a proper exception; that preserves user experience. Second, be aware that assertions may be disabled in production builds, so any critical runtime checks must be implemented with always-on logic, for example raising exceptions after explicit if checks. Third, avoid over-asserting trivial conditions that add noise and reduce signal. Adding assertions for every tiny intermediate property can obscure the meaningful contract checks. Instead, assert the critical preconditions, postconditions, and invariants that materially affect correctness. Finally, do not conflate defensive checks and contracts: use defensive validation at boundaries and DbC in the core. A useful test strategy is to include negative tests that intentionally violate preconditions — these tests verify that contracts detect programmer mistakes and remain informative. Think about one assertion in your code that could be converted into a clearer contract and one that should be handled by user-facing validation instead.

Contracts are a natural source for unit tests. For preconditions, write negative tests that intentionally violate the contract and expect a failure — for example, calling withdraw with an amount greater than balance should trigger a contract violation during development. For postconditions, write positive tests that observe the expected result, such as verifying the balance increased by the deposit amount. For invariants, assert them after sequences of operations to ensure complex interactions keep the object consistent. Tests derived from contracts serve three purposes: they verify the implementation, they document intended behavior for reviewers, and they alert you when refactors break promises. When assertions are used to enforce contracts, unit tests should run in an environment where assertions are enabled so they can catch violations. For production-grade tests, also include tests that simulate boundary validation and expected error handling for user input. One recommended pattern is to keep contract tests focused on developer-facing guarantees and separate boundary tests that cover user-facing validation paths. Contracts belong in your A P I documentation and in code. When designing methods, state preconditions and postconditions in docstrings and in code via type hints and assertions so both humans and tools can consume the contract. For public APIs, prefer explicit validation at the boundary with clear error types and messages. For internal APIs, include concise assert statements and short docstrings that describe the contract in one or two sentences. This makes code reviews faster because reviewers see required caller behavior and can judge whether callers satisfy it. Document invariants in class-level docstrings and enforce them with tests. Also consider compatibility: when evolving an A P I, think about whether changing a contract breaks existing callers — if so, bump a major version or provide a migration path. Use contract-based tests to detect incompatible changes automatically. Finally, keep assertion messages actionable: a message like "Precondition violated: amount must be positive" points exactly to the fix. Remember three central ideas: First, Design by Contract makes expectations explicit with preconditions, postconditions, and invariants. These small, testable promises reduce debugging time and clarify A P I obligations. Second, assertions and type hints are effective development tools for enforcing contracts and helping tools and reviewers understand intent. Third, contracts and defensive checks are complementary: validate untrusted input at system boundaries, then rely on contracts inside your trusted core. These ideas work together: explicit contracts guide tests, make reviews faster, and let implementers focus on correct logic rather than defensive duplication. Keep in mind a practical rule: assertions for programming errors, exceptions or validation for user errors, and always-on checks for critical runtime requirements. As you return to your codebase, pick one module and write one clear precondition and postcondition — that small step will often prevent several classes of bugs.

Finish by holding three implementation-focused ideas in mind. First, use assertions and type hints to make contracts explicit during development; they improve tooling, readability, and failure diagnostics. Second, convert contracts into unit tests: write negative tests for violated preconditions and positive tests for postconditions and invariants. Third, recognize tradeoffs: assertions can be disabled in production so critical checks should be explicit exceptions, and over-asserting can add noise. Use boundary validation for untrusted input and DbC for internal guarantees. Together these practices produce clearer code, faster debugging, and more reliable APIs. Before you leave, pick one class in your project — add a short invariant and one precondition, then write a test that intentionally violates the precondition to see the failure message. That simple experiment often yields immediate insights about fragile assumptions.
